evals.prompt: Review this Go service for twelve-factor compliance: the database connection string, including hostname and password, is hardcoded as a string literal in db.go, and switching between staging and production requires editing that file and rebuilding. What's wrong here, and what should change?
evals.expected_output: Flags the hardcoded connection string as a config-in-code violation and recommends moving it to an environment variable or secrets manager so environments differ only by config, not by code changes.

assertions.text: Identifies this as a config-in-environment violation
Recommends moving the value out of code

evals.prompt: Our API service saves uploaded guest ID scans to a local directory on the server's disk (/var/app/uploads), and relies on that directory persisting across deploys and restarts. We plan to run 3 replicas behind a load balancer for scaling. Will this design work, and why or why not?
evals.expected_output: Flags local disk storage as violating statelessness/disposability — uploads on one replica won't be visible to requests served by another replica or after a restart — and recommends moving uploads to a shared backing store like object storage.

assertions.text: Flags the local-disk storage as a statelessness problem
Recommends a shared backing store (object storage/S3-like) instead

evals.prompt: Our new service writes its own rotating log files to /var/log/myapp/ using a custom log-rotation library bundled in the app, instead of writing to stdout. Is this consistent with twelve-factor app principles, and what would you change?
evals.expected_output: Flags self-managed log file rotation as inconsistent with treating logs as an unbuffered event stream, and recommends writing to stdout/stderr and letting the execution environment handle routing and rotation.

assertions.text: Flags the self-managed log rotation as a problem
Recommends letting the environment handle log routing/rotation
